title: The beloved son (Luke 20:1–19)
hook: the tenants kill the owner's son; the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone

segments.voice: Yesterday, he wept over the city that did not know its time of visitation. Your line was if only you knew. Which place, near or far, did you hold in mind for its peace? Day five hundred seventy-two.

It's the last week, and Jesus is teaching in the temple courts every day. The leaders come with a sharp question: by what authority are you doing these things? Who gave you the right? He answers with a question of his own, about John the Baptist, and they can't answer it without trouble either way. So nobody answers. And then he tells the crowd a story. A man plants a vineyard, rents it out to tenant farmers, and goes away for a long time. At harvest he sends a servant to collect his share of the fruit. The tenants beat him and send him back with nothing. He sends a second. Same. A third. They wound him and throw him out. Today is what the owner does next.

In the King James Bible, the owner thinks out loud: "What shall I do? I will send my beloved son: it may be they will reverence him when they see him." Stop on that. Three servants beaten, and his answer is to send the person he loves most. It's not a clever plan. It's a hopeful one, maybe a foolish one. And the tenants see the son coming and reason the other way: this is the heir, kill him, and the vineyard is ours. They throw him out of the vineyard and kill him. Some in that crowd may have known the picture. In Isaiah, Israel is God's vineyard, planted with care. And the word beloved has been heard before in Luke. At the river, a voice from heaven called Jesus "my beloved Son." So Christians hear the story pointing at the one telling it. Luke says plainly who heard it as aimed at them: the chief priests and the scribes, who wanted to arrest him that hour and held back because they feared the people. Not a whole nation. A small circle of leaders in one tense week. Christians have sometimes forgotten that and turned this parable against Jewish people, and some churches have since said so with regret. Then Jesus looks at the crowd and quotes a psalm: "The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner." The builders look over a stone and toss it aside as useless. Later that very stone ends up holding the whole building together. The rejection is not the end of the story. It's the turn.
screen: `A STORY AIMED AT A FEW LEADERS.`
then, large: `THE STONE WHICH THE BUILDERS REJECTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for the rejected stone. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you set aside as useless. A person you wrote off at work. An idea you dropped because someone laughed. A part of yourself you keep hidden, the clumsy part, the quiet part. Hold it in front of you for a moment, like a builder turning over a stone. What if this is the one that holds things together? Don't decide anything. Just look at it again, more slowly than you did the first time. If you pray, you can bring it to God and leave it there. The bell holds the time.
Isaiah. The prophet whose picture of Israel as God's own vineyard lies behind the parable of the owner's last, beloved messenger.
Your line: they will respect my son. Today, give one person you'd written off a second hearing, the way the owner kept on sending. Day five hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Churches that follow a lectionary read the parable of the wicked tenants in their cycle of readings, and Psalm 118, with its rejected stone, is traditionally sung at Easter.

myth: Luke says the parable was aimed at the whole Jewish people
Luke says the chief priests and the scribes perceived it was spoken against them, and that they feared the people.
the owner sends three servants before his son
each is beaten and sent back empty. then he sends the one he loves.
the cornerstone line is Jesus quoting a psalm
it comes from Psalm 118, a psalm of thanksgiving.

fork.setup: you own the vineyard. three servants have come home beaten and empty-handed. what do you do?
options: send soldiers to throw the tenants out.
send your beloved son, hoping they'll respect him.
fork.reveal: "I will send my beloved son: it may be they will reverence him when they see him." a hopeful choice, and the tenants kill him.

original.note: Greek: beloved, dearly loved. the same word the voice from heaven uses at Jesus's baptism in Luke 3:22.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about bad tenants and a landlord.
what it means: an owner who keeps sending, last of all his beloved son, and a rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone.
what a scholar hears: the vineyard echoes Isaiah 5, and 'beloved son' echoes the voice at the baptism; Luke names the chief priests and scribes as the ones who took it personally.

notes: The carry 'they will respect my son' is a modern rendering; the KJV of Luke 20:13 reads 'reverence him'. Both are given.

Luke 20:19 names the chief priests and scribes as those who perceived the parable was against them. The script notes that the parable has been misused against Jewish people and that many churches now acknowledge this; confirm the phrasing.
Isaiah 5 vineyard background is a standard commentary link; Luke's version (20:9) is less explicit about Isaiah than Mark 12:1. Confirm.
Psalm 118:22 in the KJV reads 'refused'; Luke 20:17 KJV reads 'rejected'. The script quotes Luke.
